title: African languages, storytelling and AI at the Helsinki Book Fair
content:
Language is this year’s theme at the Helsinki Book Fair. , the University of Helsinki’s Africa Research Forum for Social Sciences and Humanities, is putting on the programme together with the and Diversity in Society and Life () research area. 

The talks look at multilingualism from several sides. In From tales to transformation: Arabic storytelling for children (Thursday 22 October, 15:00, at the stall), Professor Friederike Lüpke talks with educator Sanaa Elbehairy, who has run weekly Arabic storytelling sessions for children at Sello Library for two years. Together they discuss what stories in Arabic mean for multilingual children growing up in Finland.

title: Three Tenses of One War
content:
European security is usually drawn in the form of lines: the eastern flank, the front line in Ukraine, and the borders of NATO and the EU. But the deepest fault line in the region today runs not through space, but through time. What a government believes is at stake, and what it is prepared to concede decides which tense of the war it is living in.  
 

The first tense is the pre-war. In 2024, Poland’s Prime Minister Tusk told Europeans that they had entered a “pre-war era”. Eastern-flank governments now plan around a two-year horizon: the time Russia may need after a ceasefire to rebuild forces for a regional war, most probably in the Baltic Sea region. European intelligence officials now speak of “months, not years”. Either way, the date does the work, turning a distant threat into a schedule: conscription returns, bomb shelters are counted, and NATO’s members pledge 5 per cent of GDP on defence by 2035. This is less militarism than anticipatory securitisation, where a threat with a date on it makes extraordinary measures routine.

title: Gaiani johdattaa kestävään gastronomiaan – tule maksutta mukaan!
content:
The University of Helsinki is offering a free online course, Sustainable Gastronomy, from 27 October to 23 November 2026. The course is led by Italian agricultural scientist Dr Silvia Gaiani, who holds two doctoral degrees, and is open to students, professionals and everyone working in food culture, gastronomy and the food business.

The pilot course provides concrete tools and ideas for turning locality, seasonality and responsibility into tasty and commercially sustainable concepts.

The teaching combines practical skills with systems-level understanding: topics include food cultures, natural resource management, innovation, sustainable restaurant operations, menu development and storytelling.

Gaiani highlights the strengths of Finnish food culture – its connection to nature and the seasons, purity, simplicity, seasonality and innovation – and stresses that gastronomy always tells a story about the origin of ingredients and local value creation. The course also examines how new business models and innovations can support more sustainable food systems.

title: Thirty years of Aleksanteri: A history of change, curiosity, and connection
content:
As the Institute celebrates its 30th anniversary, its history reveals not only how the world around it has changed, but how an academic community has grown and evolved alongside it. 

When the Aleksanteri Institute was founded in 1996, Europe was still coming to terms with the end of an era.  

Only five years had passed since the collapse of the Soviet Union. Newly independent states had emerged, political systems were being reinvented, and the future of Russia and its neighbours remained uncertain. For Finland, where developments on the other side of the eastern border have often had serious implications for the country as well, understanding these transformations was especially important.  

It was against this backdrop that the Aleksanteri Institute was established at the University of Helsinki, at the initiative of Finland's Ministry of Education. Its task was ambitious: to strengthen and coordinate Finnish research and education on Russia and Eastern Europe. This meant building capacity in the field by training doctoral and MA-level students of all Finnish universities and bringing together expertise that had previously been scattered across different universities and disciplines.

title: What can a glowing fibre tell us about a medieval document?
content:
Medieval charters are more than written records. They are physical objects, carefully produced and preserved, with materials that can tell us much about the people and practices behind them. In CHARM, we also have charters that have seals attached to them with parchment strips or cords. The attachment, with the seal, helped to authenticate documents and give them authority.

But what were these threads made of? Were they linen, silk, or another fibre? And how were their colours produced?

As part of the CHARM project, we are investigating the fibres used to attach seals to medieval Finnish charters, to see if they can provide a useful additional proxy in our project.

title: Did Mendel Breed Mice?
content:
We are delighted to share a new essay from our group, published open access in . Many genetics students have heard that Mendel first studied inheritance in mice, saw the segregation of fur colour, and switched to peas only when a disapproving bishop objected to a friar watching rodents mate. It is a wonderful story, but is it true?

The paper traces the tale back to its only source, Hugo Iltis, who interviewed people who had known Mendel and reported that he kept white and grey mice in his rooms at the abbey. Iltis himself presented any crossing experiments as his own speculation. The essay sets this against the real tensions of the time, including the hostility of Bishop Schaffgotsch towards St Thomas’s Abbey, and shows that the famous remark attributed to Mendel, that the bishop did not realise plants also have sex, is a modern literary invention with no historical basis.

That Mendel kept mice is plausible, but what he did with them remains unknown. The story, the paper argues, is a fine example of how anecdotes gather around famous scientists and of the temptation to read the past through what we already know.
